nameStory: Maryland senna gets its name from the state where it was first scientifically described, though it actually grows throughout much of eastern North America. The word 'senna' comes from Arabic, referring to plants in this genus that have been used medicinally for centuries.
description: Maryland senna is a tall, graceful wildflower that can reach up to 6 feet in height, making it one of our more impressive native perennials. In summer, it produces cheerful clusters of bright yellow flowers that look like tiny golden cups. After blooming, it develops long, flat seed pods that dangle from the stems like natural wind chimes. This member of the pea family prefers wet feet and rich soil.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow flowers with 5 rounded petals arranged in loose, upright clusters at the stem tips - each flower about the size of a nickel with prominent dark stamens

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves divided into 6-10 pairs of oval leaflets arranged along a central stem, smooth to the touch and bright green with a slight sheen

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Long, flat, brown seed pods that hang downward and rattle gently when shaken, splitting open to reveal dark seeds inside

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, upright perennial that forms clumps over time, with sturdy green stems that rarely need staking despite their impressive height

habitat: Maryland senna thrives in moist to wet soils along stream banks, pond edges, and low-lying meadows throughout New England. You'll often find it in partially shaded areas or woodland edges where the soil stays consistently damp. It's occasionally spotted in rain gardens and naturalized areas where water tends to collect.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from the ground in late spring, unfurling their compound leaves as the weather warms.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with bright yellow flower clusters appearing from mid to late summer, attracting bees and butterflies.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods mature and turn brown, eventually splitting open to release seeds while leaves turn yellow before dropping.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the ground, leaving only dried seed pods and stems that provide winter interest and food for birds.

funFact: Despite being called 'Maryland' senna, this plant is so rare in New England that it's been recorded only once in the entire region - making any sighting a truly special botanical discovery!
confusionNotes: Maryland senna is most easily confused with its close relative American senna, but Maryland senna has more leaflet pairs (6-10 vs 4-8) and tends to prefer wetter soils. The yellow pea-family flowers also distinguish both sennas from other tall yellow wildflowers like goldenrods, which have much smaller, daisy-like flower heads.
contextualKnowledge: Many senna species have been used as herbal laxatives, but it's important to know that these plants can be toxic if consumed improperly. Always admire wild plants without harvesting, and never eat any plant you can't identify with 100% certainty.
compareHints: Maryland senna differs from American senna by having more pairs of leaflets per compound leaf and preferring wetter growing conditions. Both species are much taller than American sicklepod, which stays closer to 3 feet and has more triangular leaflets. The key is counting those leaflet pairs and noting the habitat - Maryland senna loves wet feet more than its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: American senna can be distinguished from its close relative Maryland senna by its hairier seed pods ("hebecarpa" means "hairy fruit") and slightly more northern range.
Unlike American senna and Maryland senna which are native New England perennials with pointed leaflets, American sicklepod is an annual with distinctly blunt, rounded leaflet tips.
